nameStory: This grass earned its name from its unusually wide leaves - 'broad-leaved' - which stand out among the typically narrow-bladed grass family. The 'panic' part comes from the Latin 'panicula,' referring to its loose, branching flower cluster that spreads out like an open hand.
description: Broad-leaved panic grass is a native perennial grass that grows in small clumps, reaching 1-3 feet tall. Unlike most grasses with thin, narrow blades, this species has notably wide, oval-shaped leaves that can be up to an inch across. It produces delicate, airy flower clusters in late spring and early summer that dance gracefully in the breeze. This woodland grass has a two-season growth pattern, looking quite different in spring versus late summer.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Distinctly broad for a grass - up to 1 inch wide and oval-shaped rather than linear. They feel smooth and have prominent parallel veins that you can easily see and feel with your finger.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Loose, open clusters of tiny purple-tinged flowers that appear in May and June. The seed head feels delicate and wispy when you gently brush your hand through it.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms small tufts or clumps rather than spreading into large patches. Plants have a distinctive two-phase growth - tall and flowering in spring, then shorter and leafier in fall.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Small, round seeds that mature in summer and often persist into fall. They're tiny but noticeable when you run the seed head between your fingers.

habitat: Look for this grass in rich, moist woodlands and forest edges throughout New England's deciduous and mixed forests. It thrives in partial shade under oak, maple, and beech trees, often growing alongside wild ginger and trout lily. You'll typically find it in well-drained but moisture-retentive soils on gentle slopes and in woodland clearings.

seasonality.spring: Tall flowering stems emerge early, producing loose purple-tinged flower clusters in May and June. This is when the grass is most noticeable and easiest to identify.
seasonality.summer: Seeds ripen and the tall stems begin to die back. The plant enters a transition phase as it prepares for its second growth period.
seasonality.fall: A completely different-looking rosette of short, broad leaves appears at ground level. This fall growth form can look like a different plant entirely.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level, leaving little trace above the snow. Look for dried seed heads that may persist in protected areas.

funFact: This grass is like a botanical shape-shifter - it grows two completely different-looking forms in the same year! The tall, flowering spring form looks so different from the short, leafy fall rosette that early botanists sometimes classified them as separate species.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with sedges due to its broad leaves, but remember that sedges have triangular stems while this grass has round, hollow stems. The leaves of broad-leaved panic grass also have the parallel veins typical of grasses, not the three-ribbed pattern of many sedges.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'panic grass,' this plant has nothing to do with panic or anxiety. The term comes from an ancient Latin word for a type of grain, showing how plant names can carry forward meanings that no longer seem obvious to modern speakers.
compareHints: Among its Dichanthelium relatives, broad-leaved panic grass stands out for having the widest leaves - most other rosette grasses have much narrower, linear blades. Deertongue has similarly broad leaves but grows much taller (up to 4 feet) and has a more robust appearance. The two-phase growth habit is shared with other rosette grasses, but the leaf width makes identification more straightforward than with narrow-leaved species.

Starved witchgrass is much more delicate and sparse than its relatives like deertongue or broad-leaved panic grass, which have wider leaves and more robust growth.
Among its many witchgrass relatives, forked witchgrass stands out for its distinctly Y-shaped branching pattern.

Among its rosette grass relatives, round-fruited rosette-panicgrass is distinguished primarily by its perfectly spherical seeds - most others like hairy rosette-panicgrass or deertongue have oval or egg-shaped seeds.
Among its many rosette grass relatives, hairy rosette-panicgrass stands out for its consistently fuzzy, velvety texture - most others like deertongue feel smooth or slightly rough.
Among its witchgrass relatives, Bosc's witchgrass tends to have broader leaves than Starved Witchgrass or Slim-leaf Witchgrass, but narrower leaves than broad-leaved panic grass.
Among its many rosette grass relatives, Slim-leaf Witchgrass stands out for having the narrowest leaves - most other Dichanthelium species have broader, more oval-shaped leaves.
Among its many Dichanthelium relatives in New England, variable witchgrass tends to be more adaptable to different moisture levels than most.
Among its witchgrass relatives, Small-fruited Witchgrass is distinguished primarily by its exceptionally tiny seeds - much smaller than deertongue or broad-leaved panic grass.
Wright's Rosette Grass differs from its relatives like deertongue and the various witchgrasses by forming more perfectly circular, compact rosettes rather than loose clumps.
Compared to its Dichanthelium relatives, slender panic grass is notably more delicate and fine-textured than broad-leaved panic grass, and lacks the dense hairiness of hairy rosette-panicgrass.
Northern witchgrass is distinguished from its Dichanthelium relatives primarily by its northern range preference and smaller overall size.

Among the many panic grass relatives in New England, velvet panicum stands out for its exceptionally soft, velvety texture - most other Dichanthelium species are hairy but not nearly as plush-feeling.
Unlike the more common deertongue with its broad leaves and dense shade tolerance, false bearded panic grass has much narrower leaves and prefers wet, open areas.

Among its many Dichanthelium relatives in New England, Heller's rosette grass stands out for its strong preference for partial shade rather than full sun, and its consistently neat rosette growth pattern.

Among the rosette grasses, Scribner's Panicgrass is distinguished by its relatively narrow rosette leaves compared to broad-leaved panic grass, and its more pointed leaf tips compared to the rounded leaves of deertongue.

Eaton's Witchgrass is distinguished from its many Dichanthelium relatives by subtle differences in leaf width, flower cluster branching patterns, and seed size - characteristics that often require expert identification.

Old-field panic grass differs from its many Dichanthelium relatives primarily by habitat preference - while species like deertongue prefer shady woodlands, old-field panic grass seeks out sunny, disturbed areas.
Among its many Dichanthelium relatives, old field panic grass is distinguished by its preference for truly open, disturbed habitats rather than woodland edges.
Among New England's rosette grasses, Lindheimer's panicgrass stands out for its nearly hairless leaves and preference for wetter soils.
Hemlock panic grass differs from its Dichanthelium relatives by its preference for coniferous rather than deciduous woods and its particularly delicate, narrow leaves.
